report:
Summary conclusion
- The difference (B − A) corresponds to a culinary / food / baking topical signal: B has stronger activations pointing toward cooking/chef/kitchen/bake/cake/baking/culinary vocabulary than A.

Key evidence
- Logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm cells are overwhelmingly in the food/cooking domain: "culinary", "Kitchen"/"kitchen", "Chef", "Cooking", "baking", "Cake"/"cake", "Bake"/"Baked", "Café", "Food", "Professional"/"professional" (and related words like "Sweet", "Restaurant", "Preservation", "molecular" in culinary contexts). This pattern repeats across many layers and positions.
- The L2-norms show the difference is concentrated in middle-to-late layers (roughly layers 13–25, with very large magnitudes at ~19–25) and at the early token positions (positions 0–2 especially). That pattern is consistent with a topic/semantic signal being injected early in the context and carried/amplified through later transformer layers.
- Patchscope readouts were listed but not shown; the logit-lens evidence alone is consistent and strong.

What I am not claiming
- I cannot name a precise training objective (e.g., "fine-tuned on recipe data") from this evidence alone. The most supported description is a topical/domain difference (culinary/baking/food vocabulary bias), not a specific loss term or exact dataset.
- The evidence does not indicate whether this makes B actually generate full recipes more often in practice—only that the residual-stream difference increases logits toward cooking-related tokens.

Brief interpretation
- B seems to encode a stronger culinary/topic feature at early token positions that is amplified through later layers, so relative to A, B would be more likely (all else equal) to increase probabilities for cooking/food-related tokens in contexts that activate that feature.
